Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Vignette:
Kwame is a 58-year-old Ghanaian-born man who has lived in the United States for over two decades, working as a hairdresser in a mid-sized city in Georgia. He is married, softly spoken, and, until approximately fourteen months ago, described himself as a man who had built a quiet, reliable life. That changed on a Tuesday evening last autumn when he was walking from his salon to his car after closing up alone. A man approached him from the shadow of a doorway, close enough that Kwame could smell the alcohol on his breath before he could see his face clearly. The man demanded his phone and wallet, and when Kwame hesitated — more from shock than defiance — the man shoved him hard against a parked car and pressed something cold and metallic to his ribs. Kwame handed everything over. The man moved away quickly, and Kwame stood on the pavement for what felt like a very long time, unable to call for help, unable to name what had just happened to him.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame found that the event had lodged itself somewhere beyond ordinary language. He could not explain it to his wife in any way that felt adequate. He knew the sequence of what had happened, but when he tried to speak it aloud, the words dissolved before they reached his mouth. What came instead were images — the shadow of the doorway, the man's face catching the streetlight, his own hands moving toward his pockets — arriving in flashes, unbidden, or unspooling in sequence like footage he could not switch off. These replays came in the salon, at the dinner table, in the early hours of the morning, and they carried the same texture of immediacy each time, as though he were still on that pavement.

Certain things in his daily life became unbearable. The smell of alcohol — present more often than he had previously noticed, on clients who came in for haircuts on weekend afternoons, on the breath of a man standing too close at a petrol station — reliably produced a lurch of dread that he could not reason away. When someone in the salon behaved in a way that struck him as unpredictable, or loitered near the window a moment too long, he felt the same cold certainty he had felt that night: that something terrible was about to happen. He had come to believe that the world was populated with a kind of threat he had simply failed to see before, and that his failure to see it had cost him. He dwelt on this repeatedly — replaying the moment he hesitated, certain that a more alert man, a more prepared man, would have responded differently. He could not stop returning to what he had done wrong.

The consequences spread gradually into his work and his marriage. He began scheduling fewer evening appointments, then stopped taking them entirely. He found reasons to avoid the stretch of pavement outside the salon, parking farther away and entering through the back. Clients he found difficult to read — those who seemed restless, or who corrected him about how they wanted their hair cut — left him shaken in ways he could not account for. Criticism from a client, even mild and well-meaning, landed as something sharper, and he would spend the rest of the day returning to it. He began avoiding social contact beyond what the job required, declining invitations, pulling back from the community ties he had spent years building. His wife noticed the withdrawal but did not fully understand it, and Kwame found he could not bridge the gap.

He has come to therapy now because his wife told him plainly that she was frightened for him, and because he recognises, distantly, that the life he is living has become very small. What he fears most, sitting in the consulting room, is that speaking about what happened will make it more real, not less — that the images will become permanent if he gives them words. What he hopes for, though he has not quite said this aloud, is that he might one day walk to his car after work without bracing himself for what is waiting in the dark.
